messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
  Negative Appraisals: Low Coping: I can't deal with even the slightest upset, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Howard is a 71-year-old married man who has worked for years as a security guard, the kind of employee who once took quiet pride in being steady, watchful, and useful. The event he circles around in treatment happened during a late shift at a downtown office building when a man entered the lobby carrying a bag and shouting before detonating an explosive device. Howard remembers the blast with terrible clarity: the flash against the glass doors, the pressure in his chest, the smell of smoke and scorched wiring, the sight of people dropping to the floor and screaming. Certain fragments remain almost painfully sharp, as if preserved outside time. At other moments, when he tries to recount the sequence from the man’s entrance to the arrival of first responders, he loses the thread entirely. He says he can see pieces “like photographs,” yet cannot make them into a full story, and sometimes he describes the scene in a flat, detached voice, as if it happened to someone else.

In the weeks afterward, what unsettled Howard most was not only what he had witnessed but what he had come to believe it said about him. He was certain that somebody else, someone more competent or quicker, would not have gotten caught in that situation. As a man who had spent his life thinking his job was to protect people, he felt he had failed in his most important role. That belief spread beyond the event itself. Small frustrations at home or at work began to feel like proof that he could no longer handle anything; he had come to believe he could not deal with even the slightest upset without coming apart inside.

Those conclusions shaped the way he began to live. Back at work, Howard started positioning himself so that he always sat with his back to the wall, scanning the whole lobby and every doorway. In restaurants with his wife, he insisted on the same seat and grew tense if he could not see the room. He watched people constantly for signs of danger—the set of a jaw, a bulky coat, a bag held too tightly—and his attention fastened especially on anyone who seemed agitated or out of place. Beneath that vigilance was a grim line of thinking that occupied him for hours: fantasies of how he might get even with the attacker, as though imagining revenge could undo the humiliation and failure he felt. To Howard, these habits made sense; if he was as vulnerable and incapable as he feared, then constant readiness seemed like the only way to prevent another disaster.

Over time those strategies did not settle him. Sitting rigidly in corners and monitoring everyone around him seemed to keep the bombing close, as if his mind never got permission to place it in the past. Details of the attack remained unnaturally vivid—the bag near the entrance, the burst of noise, the faces in the lobby—because he was repeatedly searching the present for their equivalents. His revenge-filled rumination pulled him back into the event as well, rehearsing the danger and its aftermath rather than letting it become a completed memory. Yet the more he stayed locked in these mental and physical precautions, the less coherent his account became. He could summon exact sensory fragments but not a clear beginning, middle, and end, and at times he spoke of the bombing with an eerie numbness that frightened his wife, who said it was like listening to him describe a news clip instead of the worst day of his life.

Those same habits also deepened the beliefs that had first driven them. Howard’s constant scanning left him exhausted and on edge, which he took as evidence that he truly could not handle normal stress anymore. When a customer at work approached too quickly and Howard felt his heart pound, he read that reaction not as fear but as proof of weakness. His insistence on controlling where he sat caused arguments with his wife and led him to avoid going out unless he could manage the setting, which only reinforced his sense that he was no longer the dependable husband and protector he believed he should be. Even his hours spent imagining revenge hardened the feeling that he had been reduced by the attack into someone defined by helplessness and unfinished business.

By the time he sought help, Howard was still going to work, but the job had narrowed into a daily exercise in surveillance. Every person entering the building could become a possible threat. He could not relax in public unless he had a wall behind him, and even then he was not at ease. What finally brought him in was his wife telling him that he was physically present but never really with her anymore, always watching the door, always somewhere back in that lobby. Howard says he wants to be able to sit in a room without mapping every exit and every stranger. What frightens him most is the conviction that the bombing revealed something permanent—that he failed when it mattered, and that he will never again be the man who could keep anyone safe.
